prompt.context: A friend of the interviewer owns a chain of supermarkets. While playing golf, the friend posed the question: why should he continue to centralize his company's sourcing rather than split procurement and distribution to the individual store level?
prompt.question: Why should the supermarket chain owner continue to centralize sourcing and distribution, rather than decentralizing it to the individual store level? Walk through the pros and cons of centralization and arrive at a recommendation.

clarifying_info.q: Are there specific cost targets or financial metrics to evaluate?
clarifying_info.a: No specific financials are provided; this is a qualitative, open-ended conceptual case.

clarifying_info.q: How many stores does the chain have?
clarifying_info.a: Not specified; treat it as a general multi-store supermarket chain.

clarifying_info.q: What categories of products does the chain carry?
clarifying_info.a: Not specified; assume a typical broad assortment including commodity and niche categories.

framework: Define the decision: centralized sourcing/distribution (HQ-managed) vs. decentralized (store-level procurement and distribution)
Map pros of centralization: supplier leverage, economies of scale, cost of warehouse location, staff expertise
Map cons of centralization (pros of decentralization): local demand knowledge, supplier-paid direct delivery, minimum order size constraints
Weigh the factors and identify the key deciding reason
Arrive at a recommendation with caveats

questions.prompt: What are the main pros of centralizing sourcing and distribution?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) aggregated demand lets HQ 'squeeze' suppliers for better pricing/terms; (2) economies of scale in warehouse size and operations; (3) warehouse can be sited in a low-cost area rather than on expensive store real estate; (4) store-level staff are not trained negotiators — having them procure is an extra cost with likely worse outcomes.

questions.prompt: What are the main cons of centralizing (i.e., reasons to decentralize to the store level)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify: (1) local store staff understand niche category needs (format, size, local preferences) better than HQ; (2) if suppliers deliver directly to stores, the distribution cost is borne by the supplier, not the retailer; (3) some niche or small-volume products may not be viable to order at HQ scale — store-level ordering makes them accessible.

questions.prompt: After covering the standard pros and cons, the interviewer hints there is 'something else' — a deeper or less obvious reason to centralize. What might it be?
questions.guidance: The key insight is supplier willingness and logistics feasibility: a supplier may REFUSE to ship directly to individual stores because the per-store order volume is too small to be profitable or logistically feasible (e.g., a supplier cannot fill a truck for a single small store). Centralized distribution aggregates volume to a level that makes the supplier relationship viable at all. Without centralization, the retailer may simply lose access to certain suppliers or products entirely.

brainstorming.prompt: What factors — beyond standard cost and efficiency arguments — should the owner consider when deciding whether to centralize or decentralize sourcing and distribution?

categories.name: Supplier Relationship & Power
ideas: Aggregated volume gives HQ negotiating leverage on price, payment terms, and service levels
Small per-store volumes may make the retailer an unattractive customer — some suppliers may decline to serve
Centralization enables consistent supplier contracts and compliance monitoring

categories.name: Logistics & Feasibility
ideas: Suppliers may lack trucks or capacity to serve many small locations
Minimum viable shipment size (full truckload vs. LTL) affects whether direct-to-store delivery is even possible
Central warehouse can optimize inbound and outbound routing

categories.name: Cost Structure
ideas: Centralized warehouse in a low-cost area reduces real estate cost
Economies of scale in warehouse labor, equipment, and technology
Store-level procurement staff is a duplicated headcount cost

categories.name: Product & Category Considerations
ideas: Niche or locally-demanded products may need store-level discretion
Perishables with fast demand swings may benefit from store-level flexibility
Private-label or exclusive supplier programs typically require central coordination

categories.name: Organizational Capability
ideas: Store managers and staff typically lack procurement training and negotiation skills
Centralized buying teams develop specialized expertise over time
Technology (ERP, demand forecasting) is easier to deploy centrally

recommendation: Maintain centralized sourcing and distribution as the primary model

The decisive reason beyond cost and scale is that many suppliers will not ship to individual stores due to insufficient order volumes — centralization is necessary to retain access to these suppliers and products
Layer in selective store-level discretion only for niche, locally-specific, or perishable categories where local knowledge clearly outweighs scale benefits
risks: Centralized model may be slower to respond to store-specific or local demand shifts
Risk of over-standardization that alienates local customer preferences
Single point of failure in the central warehouse (operational or disaster risk)
next_steps: Audit current supplier base to identify which suppliers require minimum order volumes incompatible with store-level procurement
Quantify the cost savings from centralized purchasing and warehouse economies of scale
Identify a short list of category exceptions where store-level procurement adds demonstrable value and pilot a hybrid model
